segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: My brothers and sisters, surely you do not hold faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ while showing favoritism?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if a man with gold rings and fine clothes comes into your assembly, and a poor man in filthy clothes also comes in,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and you look with favor on the one wearing the fine clothes and say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You sit here in a good place,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to the poor man you say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You stand, or sit down there by my footstool,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: have you not made distinctions among yourselves and become judges with evil reasoning?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Listen, my dear brothers and sisters. Has God not chosen those who are poor in the eyes of the world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom that he promised to those who love him?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you have dishonored the poor man. Is it not the rich who oppress you, and they who drag you into the courts?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Is it not they who blaspheme the good name that was invoked over you?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If, however, you are carrying out the royal law in line with the Scripture,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: you are doing well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if you show favoritism, you are committing sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at one point has become guilty of all of it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the one who said,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Do not commit adultery,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: also said,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Do not murder.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now if you do not commit adultery but do murder, you have become a transgressor of the law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So speak and so act as people who are going to be judged by a law of freedom.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For judgment is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy. Mercy triumphs over judgment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What good is it, my brothers and sisters, if someone says they have faith but does not have works? Can that faith save them?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If a brother or sister is poorly clothed and lacks daily food,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and one of you says to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Go in peace; keep warm and eat your fill,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but you do not give them what the body needs, what good is it?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So too faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But someone will say,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “You have faith and I have works.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Show me your faith apart from works, and I will show you my faith by my works.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You believe that God is one? You do well. Even the demons believe—and shudder.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do you want to be shown, you senseless person, that faith apart from works does not work?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Was not Abraham our father justified by works when he offered his son Isaac on the altar?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You see that faith was working together with his works, and by the works faith was made perfect,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and the Scripture was fulfilled that says,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he was called a friend of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You see that a person is justified by works and not by faith alone.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way, was not Rahab the prostitute also justified by works when she welcomed the messengers and sent them out by a different road?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For just as the body apart from the spirit is dead, so also faith apart from works is dead.

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and James is writing to whole communities. “Brothers” alone now suggests to an English reader that only men are addressed. Where James means a single man or woman he says so, as in verse 15.

The Greek can be read either as a prohibition (“do not hold the faith … with favoritism”) or as a question expecting the answer “no.” Most English versions choose the command. The Greek edition translated here punctuates the sentence as a question, and this translation follows it. The practical force is much the same either way.

notes.phrase: faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ
notes.traditional: the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory
notes.note: The Greek is literally “the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ of glory.” Most interpreters understand “faith of” as faith directed toward Jesus, but some take it as the faith or faithfulness that Jesus himself showed. The words “of glory” are also awkward: they may describe Jesus as glorious, name him “the Lord of glory,” or stand alongside his name as a title, “the Glory.”

The Greek word is the one elsewhere rendered “synagogue.” It meant a gathering or the place where one was held. James uses it here for the meeting of Jesus’ followers, which suggests a community still at home in Jewish vocabulary.

The verb can also mean “to be divided” or “to waver,” as it does in 1:6. On that reading James asks, “Are you not divided within yourselves?”, meaning torn between faith and the world’s standards. Either sense fits the context, and James may intend both.

notes.phrase: the good name that was invoked over you
notes.traditional: that worthy name by which you are called
notes.note: To have a name “called over” someone is an idiom from the Greek Old Testament marking that person as the property of the one named, as Israel belonged to God. Most interpreters take the name here to be that of Jesus, perhaps spoken over believers at baptism.

The Greek word covers both complete nakedness and being inadequately dressed, for example wearing only an undergarment or rags. The reply “keep warm” in the next verse shows that lack of adequate clothing is the point. Several modern versions translate similarly.

notes.phrase: You have faith and I have works
notes.note: Ancient manuscripts had no quotation marks, and it is disputed where the imagined speaker’s words end and who “you” and “I” are. Since James himself champions works, the objector is hard to place. This translation follows the common view that the objector means “one person has faith, another has works,” as if the two could be separated, and that James replies from “Show me” onward. Others extend the quotation further or treat the speaker as an ally of James.

This is the central confession of Judaism, drawn from Deuteronomy 6:4 and recited daily. James grants that the belief is correct. His point is that correct belief alone is something even demons share.

notes.traditional: is useless / is barren (KJV: is dead)
notes.note: The Greek adjective means “idle, not working, unproductive,” and it echoes the word for “works” in the same clause. “Does not work” keeps the pun, where the usual “useless” loses it. Some manuscripts read “dead” here, as in verses 17 and 26, which is the source of the King James wording. “Idle” is widely judged to be the earlier reading.

Greek has one word-family where English has two, so “justified” here and “righteousness” in verse 23 share a root. The verb can mean “declare to be in the right” or “show to be in the right, vindicate.” Many interpreters hold that James uses it in the second sense, of Abraham’s faith being proved genuine by what he did, and so does not contradict Paul’s statement that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. Others see a real difference of emphasis between the two writers.

The verb means to bring something to its goal or finished state, not to remove flaws. James’s point is that Abraham’s faith reached its full, intended form in what he did. Some versions translate “was completed” or “was brought to completion.”

candidates.reason: The plural address recurs in almost every letter, and translators divide between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters,” so readers would notice variation between chapters.
“Works,” “deeds” and “actions” are all defensible, but the James–Paul discussion depends on the same English word appearing in both.
Genesis 15:6 is quoted here, in Romans 4 and in Galatians 3, and “credited,” “counted” and “reckoned” should not vary between them.
Whether to capitalize when the Mosaic law is meant but qualified (“the whole law,” “law of freedom,” “royal law”) needs one rule across James, Paul and Hebrews.
It is normally “synagogue,” but here and in a few other places it names a gathering, possibly a Christian one, and the boundary should be fixed once.
